title: The score that resets itself
brief: In the fruit-catch game the score goes up when you catch an apple, then drops back to zero a moment later.
code:
when green flag clicked
forever
  set [score v] to (0)
  if <touching [apple v]?> then
    change [score v] by (1)
  end
end
expect: Catching an apple adds one point and the score keeps growing.
happened: The score flickers to 1 and snaps back to 0, so it can never climb.
evidence: Tick the score variable so it shows on stage. Watch it for two seconds without catching anything: it is being set back to 0 by the loop.
hint: One of these blocks should run once at the start, not on every pass of the forever loop.
explain: The `set score to 0` block sits inside the forever loop, so it runs about 30 times a second and wipes the score before you can see it. Resetting belongs outside the loop.
answer: Move `set [score v] to (0)` above the forever block so it runs once when the game starts. Keep only `change [score v] by (1)` inside the loop.

title: The coin you walk straight through
brief: In the Pygame catch game the coin slides across the screen, but pressing the arrow keys into it does nothing.
code:
coin_x = 300
coin_rect = coin.get_rect(topleft=(coin_x, 100))

while running:
    coin_x -= 3
    # coin is drawn at the new position, but the rect never moves
    if player_rect.colliderect(coin_rect):
        score += 1
expect: Reaching the coin adds a point.
happened: The sprite passes over the coin and the score stays at 0 unless you touch the spot where the coin started.
evidence: Print `coin_rect.topleft` and `coin_x` on the same line. Once the coin has moved, the two numbers disagree.
hint: The rectangle you test against and the rectangle you draw are not the same rectangle after the first frame.
explain: `coin.get_rect()` copies the position once. Moving `coin_x` changes where the image is drawn, but `coin_rect` keeps the very first coordinates, so the collision check looks at an empty patch of screen.
answer: Rebuild or move the rect after the coin moves: `coin_rect.x = coin_x` (or `coin_rect = coin.get_rect(topleft=(coin_x, 100))`) before the `colliderect` check.

title: The game that speeds up every time you click
brief: The player moves faster and faster each time you press the button, until the whole game blurs.
expect: One animation loop moves the player at a steady pace.
happened: Every click adds another loop, so the player moves twice as far with two loops, three times with three.
evidence: Add a counter inside `draw` and log it once a second. After two clicks the count is two or three times higher than after one.
hint: Count how many times a loop is allowed to start.
explain: Each click starts more loops and never stops the old one. `setInterval(draw, 16)` plus a fresh `requestAnimationFrame(draw)` gives you two loops per click, all calling `update()`.
answer: Start the loop once, outside the click handler: `requestAnimationFrame(draw);` runs a single loop because each frame schedules exactly one more. Remove the `setInterval` line.

title: The hit points that never reach zero
brief: The hero takes damage, but the game over screen never appears even when the hearts are empty.
expect: The game ends when health drops to zero or below.
happened: Health falls past 0 to -10 and the hero keeps playing, because the last hit skipped right over 0.
evidence: Print `health` after each hit. Once it shows a negative number you know the equality check missed the moment it mattered.
hint: A single hit is rarely exactly the amount of health left.
explain: `health == 0` is only true at one exact value. If the last hit deals 20 damage at 15 health, health jumps to -5 and never equals 0. Checking a range fixes it.
answer: Change the condition to `if (health <= 0) { gameOver(); }` and clamp the value with `health = Math.max(0, health)` if you want the bar to stop at empty.

title: The function that changes a copy
brief: The player collides with the spike, the damage code runs, but the health bar on screen does not move.
happened: The print inside the function shows 90, the print in `main` shows 100.
evidence: Those two numbers are the evidence: the function changed its own copy, not the player's health.
hint: Look at how the parameter is passed.
explain: `takeDamage(int health)` takes the number by value, so C++ copies 100 into a new local variable. Changing the copy leaves `playerHealth` untouched. Passing by reference shares the original.
answer: Take a reference: `void takeDamage(int& health) { health -= 10; }`. The `&` makes the parameter point at the caller's variable.

title: The player who walks through walls
brief: The character moves, but it slides straight through the level walls instead of stopping.
expect: The player stops when it reaches a wall.
happened: The player passes through the wall and keeps going off the edge of the level.
evidence: Print `position.x` every frame. It keeps increasing past the wall's x position, so nothing is blocking the movement.
hint: A CharacterBody2D has a built-in movement call that handles collisions. Are you using it?
explain: `position.x +=` moves the node directly and ignores physics. `move_and_slide()` reads the `velocity` variable and stops the body at collisions, which is why every CharacterBody2D example sets velocity first.
answer:
Set the velocity and let the engine move the body:
```
velocity.x = direction * speed
velocity.y += gravity * delta
move_and_slide()
```

title: The jump that never comes back down
brief: On some computers the character jumps once and then keeps flying upward, and on slower machines it barely jumps at all.
expect: The character jumps to a fixed height and falls back down.
happened: The height changes from one computer to another, and holding space flaps the character upward.
evidence: Log `rb.velocity.y` in `FixedUpdate` and in `Update`. The value keeps being reset before gravity has a chance to pull it down.
hint: Physics work belongs in one specific update method, and a jump needs a check that you are on the ground.
explain: Setting velocity every frame in `Update` fights gravity and runs at the monitor's frame rate, so the jump height depends on the machine. A grounded check stops repeated jumps, and physics belongs in `FixedUpdate`.

title: The score that never wins
brief: Collecting all ten coins should show the win message, but the build fails with an error instead.
expect: The win message appears at ten coins.
happened: The project will not build, and the error points at this line.
evidence: Read the build error: it names the line and says it found an unexpected symbol near '='.
hint: Lua uses a different symbol for comparing two values than for storing one.
explain: In Lua a single `=` assigns a value. Comparing needs `==`. The compiler reads `score = 10` as an assignment inside a condition and rejects it.
answer: Use a comparison: `if score == 10 then`. If the win screen already appeared you can also guard it with `if score >= 10 and not won then`.

title: The extra life
brief: The player has three lives, but after the third mistake the game keeps going instead of ending.
code:
lives = 3

function lose_life()
  lives -= 1
  if lives < 0 then
    game_over()
  end
end
expect: The game ends after the third mistake.
happened: The player gets a fourth try, because after three mistakes lives is 0 and the check never fires.
evidence: Print `lives` after each mistake: it counts 2, 1, 0 and the game is still running.
hint: Decide what zero means before you write the comparison.
explain: Subtracting first and then asking for `< 0` builds in one spare life. With three lives you want the game to end the moment the counter reaches zero.
answer: Use `if lives <= 0 then game_over() end`, or check `if lives == 0` after the subtraction. Both end the run on the third mistake.

title: The HUD that always shows zero
brief: The player collects coins and the counter on the HUD stays at 0, even though the pickup sound plays.
happened: Each object has its own `score` variable, so the player counts up while the HUD reads its own zero.
evidence: Draw `score` in both objects side by side. The player shows 3, the HUD shows 0, which means they are not looking at the same value.
hint: Where does a variable live when two different objects need to read it?
explain: In GameMaker a bare `score` belongs to the instance that reads it. The player's counter and the HUD's counter are different variables with the same name. A global is shared across every instance.
answer: Use a global in both places: `global.score += 1;` on pickup and `draw_text(20, 20, string(global.score));` in the HUD. Initialise it once with `global.score = 0;` in a controller or game start event.

title: The coin that cannot be touched
brief: A coin is created by script, but walking into it does nothing and it never appears in the level.
code:
local coin = Instance.new("Part")
coin.Size = Vector3.new(2, 2, 2)
coin.Position = Vector3.new(0, 5, 0)

coin.Touched:Connect(function(hit)
    print("coin collected")
end)
expect: The coin appears in the world and the touch message prints.
happened: No coin shows up and nothing prints, even when the player stands in that spot.
evidence: Print `coin.Parent` right after the script runs. If it is nil, the part exists in memory but not in the world.
hint: Creating an object is not the same as putting it in the game.
explain: `Instance.new` builds the part but leaves it detached. Nothing is drawn and nothing can touch it until it has a parent. Setting its position also usually wants `Anchored = true` so it stays put.
answer: Add `coin.Anchored = true` and `coin.Parent = workspace` after setting the properties, before connecting `Touched`.

title: The level that ends on the first coin
brief: The level should finish at 10 coins, but it switches to the win scene as soon as the player picks up one.
code:
Conditions:
  Variable score >= 10
Actions:
  Change the scene to "Win"
expect: The win scene loads when the score reaches 10.
happened: It loads at score 1, and keeps trying to load every frame after that.
evidence: Show the `score` value on screen. If it reads 1 and the condition still passes, the variable is text, so "1" is being compared as a word and wins.
hint: Check the type of the variable before you check the logic.
explain: A variable created as text compares letter by letter, so "1" sorts after "10" and passes `>= 10`. Numbers only compare by size. Add the Trigger Once condition so the scene change cannot repeat.
answer: Recreate `score` as a number, initialise it to 0, and add Trigger Once to the win event so the scene changes exactly one time.

title: The score that changes a copy
brief: The coin disappears when you touch it, but the HUD still shows 0.
code:
Event ActorBeginOverlap (Coin)
  -> Cast To BP_Player
  -> Add (LocalScore + 1)
  -> Set LocalScore
  -> Update HUD
expect: Collecting a coin adds 1 to the score on the HUD.
happened: The coin vanishes, the Print String shows 1, but the HUD stays at 0.
evidence: Add a Print String after the Add node, then print the player Score. One says 1, the other says 0.
hint: Follow the wire from the Add node back to the variable. Is it the same variable the HUD reads?
explain: The graph adds to a local variable, not the player Score. The HUD reads the player, so it never sees the change.
answer: Get the player character, `Set Score = Score + 1`, then call the HUD update event. Wire the coin overlap into that chain.

title: The recipe that never loads
brief: The item exists, but the recipe never appears in the recipe book.
expect: The recipe shows in the recipe book and crafts the gem.
happened: The item loads, but the recipe is missing and nothing can craft it.
evidence: Search the game log for CrystalMod. It says the recipe path contains a character that is not allowed.
hint: Look at the folder name and the namespace. Compare them with the path rules for your Minecraft version.
explain: Resource and data paths must be lowercase. `CrystalMod` with a capital letter stops the recipe from loading, even though the item still works.
answer: Rename the package, the data folder and the namespace to `crystalmod` in lowercase, update the recipe path, then press F3+T.

title: The punch that goes to an empty state
brief: The fighter loads and moves, but pressing punch does nothing.
code:
[Command]
name = "punch"
command = x

[State -1]
type = ChangeState
value = 200
expect: Pressing punch plays an attack animation and can hit the opponent.
happened: Nothing happens. The fighter stays idle.
evidence: Turn on the MUGEN debug display. The command is detected, but the state change goes to an empty state.
hint: Compare the state number in ChangeState with the [Statedef] numbers in the cns file.
explain: The command changes to state 200, but the cns defines state 2000. The fighter changes to a state that does not exist, so it stays idle.
answer: Change `value = 200` to `value = 2000`, or add a matching `[Statedef 200]` with the punch animation.

title: The plugin that is never listed
brief: The plugin file looks right, but OpenRCT2 never lists it.
expect: The plugin appears in the in-game plugin list and shows your first message.
happened: The plugin is not listed at all.
evidence: Open the OpenRCT2 plugin log. Your plugin is not mentioned, so the game never found the folder.
hint: Check the folder name OpenRCT2 scans and the main entry in plugin.json.
explain: OpenRCT2 scans `plugin`, singular. A folder called `plugins` is ignored, so the plugin never loads.
answer: Move it to `OpenRCT2/plugin/swim-rescue/` and make `plugin.json` main point at the JS file that calls `registerPlugin`.

title: The tile that loads as a blank
brief: The mod loads, but the new tile is blank.
expect: The new tile shows your art in the world.
happened: The mod loads but the tile is empty, or SMAPI reports a missing file.
evidence: Read the SMAPI console. It cannot find `assets/tiles.png`; the file in the folder is `Tiles.png`.
hint: Compare the path in content.json with the real filename, including capitals.
explain: Paths are case sensitive for many players. Windows may hide the mismatch, but a Mac or Linux player sees a missing file.
answer: Rename the file to `assets/tiles.png` in lowercase, update content.json if needed, rebuild and reload the mod.

title: The item that places dirt
brief: The custom item loads, but using it places dirt instead of your tile.
expect: Using the item places your custom tile.
evidence: Check `Item.createTile` in SetDefaults. It points at the vanilla dirt id, not your tile type.
hint: Find createTile and see which tile type it names.
explain: The item is still pointing at the vanilla dirt tile. It needs your modded tile type instead.
answer: Set `Item.createTile = ModContent.TileType<MyCustomTile>();` and make sure the tile class is registered.
